issues.description: Mode switch complects two read loops with different semantics into one function
issues.detail: The function now has two distinct state machines tangled together: a non-blocking poll-and-read loop for 'waiting for the first byte', and a blocking drain loop for 'reading the rest'. These are two different concerns with two different time models (event-driven wait vs. synchronous drain) sharing one fd and one accumulator. The complecting hides the fact that what you actually want is a small state machine: WAITING_FOR_FIRST_BYTE -> DRAINING -> DONE. Decompose into two named helpers (e.g. wait_for_first_chunk(fd, command_obj, timeout) and drain_until_eof(fd)) and the control flow becomes obvious; the inner while True / break / outer break disappears.

issues.description: fd mode is a mutable place; the function mutates it and never restores it
issues.detail: fcntl(F_SETFL, flags & ~O_NONBLOCK) mutates global state on the file descriptor with no scoping. If the caller passed in an fd they expect to remain non-blocking, or if an exception fires inside the drain loop, the fd is left in blocking mode and the next consumer inherits that surprise. This is place-oriented programming at the OS layer: the fd's mode is a value-over-time with no explicit ownership. Wrap the mode change in a contextmanager (set_blocking(fd)) with try/finally, or open a fresh fd for the drain phase. Either way, make the time semantics of the mode change explicit.

issues.description: Timeout and process-exit safety net silently deleted along with the bug
issues.detail: The prior code had two genuinely essential behaviors: (a) detect that the writer process has exited so we don't hang on a half-closed FIFO on MacOS, and (b) bail out on BlockingIOError when content already exists. Both were removed in favor of 'once we see one byte, trust POSIX blocking read to EOF.' That trust is well-founded for a well-behaved writer, but if the subprocess crashes mid-write after sending one chunk, the blocking read() inside the inner loop will now wait forever with no poll, no timeout, and no check_process_exited. The pass branches on lines 155 and 159 are dead code that used to carry real safety. Either prove the writer can never half-close-then-die after first byte, or keep a periodic poll with timeout inside the drain loop.

issues.description: The two pass branches are residue, not code
issues.detail: Lines 155 and 159 are now literally pass. They are scar tissue from the deleted logic and signal to the reader that something used to live here. Either collapse the try/except so the empty branches disappear, or invert the control flow (read first, branch on result) so the structure matches the new two-phase intent. Right now the shape of the function still looks like the old single-loop design with bandages.

issues.description: The real value here is 'one complete message'; the abstraction is still 'a loop that accumulates bytes'
issues.detail: What this code is about, in Hickey terms: a single value (the complete JSON payload) produced by a writer, consumed once by a reader, with a time boundary marked by writer-close. The current shape exposes the time-handling (poll, nonblock, fcntl, drain) at the same level as the value-handling (content += chunk). A cleaner decomposition is a generator/iterator that yields chunks until EOF, with the policy (how to wait, how to detect crash, how to time out) injected. Then the caller just does b''.join(iter_fifo(fd, command_obj)) and json.loads it. The fix as written solves the truncation bug but leaves the abstraction at the wrong altitude.

review.summary: The fix correctly identifies the root cause — non-blocking reads racing with kernel pipe buffers after writer close — and the POSIX-blocking-read drain is the right primitive. But the patch is EASY-NOT-SIMPLE: it bolts a second read loop with different time semantics inside the first, mutates the fd's mode as a side-effecting place with no restoration, and silently drops the prior MacOS-half-close and process-exit safety nets without proving they were never essential. The two pass branches are visible scar tissue. Decompose into wait_for_first_chunk + drain_until_eof, scope the mode change in a contextmanager, and decide deliberately whether the deleted process-exit check belongs inside the drain loop. The question that should have been asked first: what is the value here, and where does the time boundary actually live — in the fd, in the writer's exit, or in the message itself?
